answer.exemplar: Below the static limit the material returns to its original length on unloading, so extension is proportional to force and F equals k times x. Past that limit the material yields and takes a permanent set, so part of the extension no longer recovers, the response is no longer linear, and no single constant k describes the spring over that whole range.

questions.explanation: A good answer mentions permanent deformation and the loss of proportionality, and notes that the spring constant is valid only below the limit. An answer saying the spring is broken is wrong, since a yielded spring is still intact and can still be used within its elastic range.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the extension when the force is removed again.

answer.exemplar: Damping removes a fraction of the stored energy every cycle, so a heavily damped system has less energy to return to the drive and the peak amplitude falls. Because energy has already been lost by the time the drive is detuned, the response stays noticeable over a wider band of driving frequencies, so the peak is lower and broader while the undamped natural frequency is unchanged.

questions.explanation: A good answer links the height of the peak to the energy available per cycle and the width to how fast that energy is lost, and notes that the natural frequency still comes from the mass and the spring. An answer claiming damping lowers the natural frequency is wrong, since it only reduces the size of the response.
questions.hint: Compare the energy available at the peak with the energy lost each cycle.
